name: f1-status-line-v1
operator: recombine (cross-branch, stagnation slot): same rules, new intermediate representation
learning_goal: Does an explicit intermediate representation help a weaker reader carry out the same rules more faithfully than prose, at no extra token cost? The representation is a fixed three-slot status line followed by need, then goal, then option. The question is contrarian to P20 ('fewer reasoning steps always execute better'). Comparing this policy with f1-risk-signal-v1 (the same rules in prose) answers it for Haiku. An opus~100k or DeepSeek cell later tells whether the added structure transfers (P25/P26).
card_choice: P22 matches the symptom in the playbook's table, 'the cheap actor ignores instructions' and disordered reasoning: F1's rules exist but are skipped or reordered. P20 is already tested by f1-core-v1. P21 (one main priority) would drop the balance that transfers across actors (Problem A) and is close to f7-promotion-drive's concentration (45.2). P25 is an evaluation card that needs other actors' runs rather than new policy text.
hypothesis: F1's losses come from execution, not from missing strategy. The rules exist, but the actor skips or reorders them: Defuse after 50% of risk signals, Lay low at full Health against the Lay-low guard, Watch and Fine labels never written. A status line filled every turn makes rule execution consistent for a small model. Its slots are the Act dimensions, Risk calm or raised (F3's named signal state, borrowed as a label only) and the Weakest. A strict need order (Act, then raised Risk, then Weakest), each need mapped to its Energy, story and main-action response, does the rest. The policy should lift completion and mean quantitative_score over F1 and match or beat f1-risk-signal-v1, which has the same rules in prose.
change: The decision rules of f1-risk-signal-v1 reorganised as need, goal, option (P22). Step 2 fills 'Act: <dimensions or none> | Risk: calm or raised | Weakest: <statistic>'. Step 3 fixes the need order. The note becomes '<status line> → need → why this option'. The rules are grouped under the need they serve (Act, Risk raised, Weakest, Always) instead of under decision types. From F3-lean (cross-branch) it takes only a named risk state written at the start of every note. F3's Escalating mode, its Lay-low response, its weak-review plan and its step-down rule are not taken, because opus~100k plays the F3 family badly (Problem A). 326 words against F1's 486.
predicted_behaviour: At least 90% of notes start with the three-slot status line. The action matches the named need in at least 90% of decisions: Act leads to the recovery or maintenance for that dimension, raised Risk to Defuse legacy risk in the next Energy phase, otherwise the Weakest. That agreement is higher than in F1 or f1-risk-signal-v1. Defuse after at least 85% of risk signals. No Lay low while Health is not Act. Notes no longer than F1's mean of about 124 characters, because the line replaces free prose. At least 3 of 4 runs complete, and mean quantitative_score is at least the parent's 8-run mean (58.9).
refutation: Refuted if the status line is written but actions disagree with the named need as often as in f1-risk-signal-v1 or F1: the representation is filled in but not used. Also refuted if notes grow and the 4-run mean quantitative_score falls more than 8 points below the parent's 8-run mean: the structure costs more than it gives. A Haiku win shows only that Haiku benefits; a claim for the target model needs opus~100k or DeepSeek cells (P26).
notes: Stall slot of block 5: the leader's posterior fell 61.3 to 54.6, so the stagnation rule fires. Top rung of the nested ladder f1-core-v1, f1-risk-signal-v1, f1-status-line-v1, so each step changes one thing: subtraction, then the risk trigger, then the representation. The status line uses no numbers or quoted game text; 'low' and 'near zero' are qualitative and the 0–10 range is published. No months, review cadence or calendar triggers. Family f1-steady-balance with parents from two families, as allowed for a cross-branch slot.
